title: Tibetan Ice May Preserve the Last Ice Age
paragraphs: Researchers led by Ohio State University have found signs that an ice cap in northwest Tibet may hold ice from the last ice age. The study, published in Science Advances, looks at the Guliya ice cap on the Tibetan Plateau.

Ice cores were drilled there in 1992 and 2015, and both show very similar oxygen isotope patterns. This suggests that the climate signals in the ice are consistent. To date the ice, the team looked for traces of beryllium and chlorine left by a magnetic field event more than 41,000 years ago. They then compared their results with records from caves nearby.

Earlier research suggested that the record stopped about 12,000 years ago. Now the team estimates that it may reach back well over 128,000 years. However, this age is an estimate based on comparisons, not a direct measurement, and the scientists plan to analyse more samples. The work was funded by the US National Science Foundation.

questions.q: What did the 1992 and 2015 cores have in common?
questions.a: They showed very similar oxygen isotope patterns.

questions.q: How did the team estimate the age of the ice?
questions.a: They found traces of a magnetic field event and compared them with cave records.

questions.q: Why is the age not certain?
questions.a: It is an estimate based on comparisons, not a direct measurement.
